structure.title: Book I · A visit gets out of hand
structure.text: Socrates goes down to the port for a festival. In an elderly merchant's house, the question of paying one's debts becomes a quarrel about whose interests a just man actually serves. The host leaves to attend a sacrifice. His money and his answers stay under examination.

structure.title: Books II–IV · Build a city to see inside a man
structure.text: Two brothers demand a defence of justice that would hold even if nobody knew how a man behaved. Socrates proposes looking at a city first, on the chance that justice will be easier to read there in larger letters. Feeding and defending it soon brings teachers and poets under scrutiny.

structure.title: Books V–VII · Who could govern it?
structure.text: The company's objections force Socrates to explain how guardians might live and why anyone trained to seek truth would return to political life. The cave belongs inside this dispute about education and obligation.

structure.title: Books VIII–X · Put the tyrant beside the just man
structure.text: Forms of government decline alongside portraits of the people at home in each. The argument finally returns to pleasure, poetry and the fate of a soul, testing by several measures the initial boast that injustice pays.

people.name: Socrates
people.text: He tells the whole conversation himself, beginning with a festival evening at a friend's house. When the others demand to know whether justice is worth having for its own sake, he proposes to look for it first in an imagined city.

people.name: Thrasymachus
people.role: A paid teacher ready to interrupt
people.text: He wants an answer from Socrates for once. His claim about the stronger party gives the conversation an adversary with a practical question. Who writes the laws that obedient people call just?

people.name: Glaucon and Adeimantus
people.text: Both want Socrates to succeed. To prevent an easy victory, they give the case for injustice a better hearing than its first advocate did, including everything a parent tells a child about the rewards of a good reputation.

context.title: City and soul
context.text: The city is constructed for an investigation into the individual. Much hangs on whether a division of labour among citizens can illuminate the way one person's anger, appetite and judgment pull against one another.

notice.text: Listen for the terms of the wager.
notice.why: Glaucon gives an unjust man the reputation of perfect justice. Each reward Socrates later offers must face the possibility that the wrong man could collect it.
Arguments about censorship begin with bedtime stories. The guardians may absorb a picture of what deserves fear or admiration years before they can defend an opinion of their own.

opening: Imagine a ring that lets its owner become invisible. With punishment removed, why would anyone remain just? Plato refuses to let Socrates answer with a reassuring speech about being good. He has to defend justice against people who suspect morality is a bargain the weak impose on the strong. The argument grows into a proposed city whose rulers control education, poetry, and family life. Following it means watching an attempt to secure human goodness acquire powers that should make its readers uneasy.
